title: Who Touched That File? Linux Auditing with auditd
intro: Logs record what applications choose to log. The kernel audit system (auditd) records what actually happened: which user and process opened, changed, or executed what. It's required by most compliance standards, and it's what answers 'who changed /etc/passwd?' after an incident.

steps.prompt: List the audit rules currently loaded.
steps.explanation: auditd is running but watching nothing.
steps.why: auditd running with no rules gives false comfort: nothing is being recorded. Rules can be added live with auditctl (lost on reboot) or persistently in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules.

steps.prompt: Watch /etc/passwd for writes and attribute changes, tagging events with the key 'identity'.
steps.explanation: Any write (w) or attribute change (a) to /etc/passwd is now recorded.
steps.why: -p selects permissions to watch: r(ead), w(rite), x(ecute), a(ttribute change). The key (-k) is a label for searching later. Watch the identity files (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, /etc/sudoers) at minimum; the CIS benchmark lists the full set.

steps.prompt: Later, find every event with the key 'identity' from today, with numeric ids translated to names.
steps.fake_output:
type=SYSCALL msg=audit(09/28/2026 03:16:40.112:4411) : arch=x86_64 syscall=openat success=yes exe=/usr/sbin/useradd auid=root uid=root comm=useradd key=identity
type=PATH msg=audit(09/28/2026 03:16:40.112:4411) : name=/etc/passwd nametype=NORMAL
steps.explanation: At 03:16:40, useradd modified /etc/passwd, run by a session whose login user (auid) was root.
steps.why: -i interprets numeric UIDs and syscalls into names. The key field is auid, the 'audit user id': the account that originally logged in, which stays the same through sudo and su. It answers 'which human did this', which plain uid can't.

steps.prompt: Get a summary report of failed authentication attempts from the audit log.
steps.explanation: Failed root logins from 185.220.101.4 just before the 03:16 change.
steps.why: aureport gives summaries (auth, logins, executables, anomalies) for triage, and ausearch gives the detail. Together they rebuild a timeline: failed logins, then a successful one, then an account created, which is the sequence behind mystery-linux-006.

steps.prompt: Make the rule permanent: after adding '-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity' to /etc/audit/rules.d/identity.rules, load all rule files.
steps.fake_output:
No rules
enabled 1
failure 1
pid 612
rate_limit 0
backlog_limit 8192
(rules.d/*.rules compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules and loaded)
steps.why: augenrules merges rules.d/ into audit.rules and loads them. Ship the audit logs off the host (to your SIEM or log platform): an attacker with root can delete local audit logs, and remote copies are what make the audit trail trustworthy.
